posts.title: ACID Properties Explained: How SQL Databases Guarantee Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability
posts.subtitle: From WAL and MVCC to fsync and isolation levels — the internals behind every ACID guarantee in PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, and SQL Server.
posts.brief: ACID is four orthogonal guarantees that every SQL transaction must provide. Atomicity says all-or-nothing: PostgreSQL implements it via WAL rollback; MySQL InnoDB via undo logs. Consistency says constraints always hold: the database rejects any write that violates a `CHECK`, `FOREIGN KEY`, or `NOT NULL`. Isolation says concurrent transactions cannot see each other's intermediate states: PostgreSQL uses MVCC + Serializable Snapshot Isolation; MySQL InnoDB uses MVCC + Two-Phase Locking. Durability says committed data survives crashes: every major database writes to a write-ahead log and calls `fsync` before acknowledging a commit. Know which property protects which failure class — and know the configuration knobs that let you trade durability for throughput when the workload permits.

posts.title: ACID Transactions in Distributed Databases: DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, and Spanner Compared
posts.subtitle: How modern NoSQL databases achieve atomicity and isolation without a single machine
posts.brief: ACID transactions in distributed databases are not equal. DynamoDB provides multi-item atomicity scoped to 25 items using two-phase commit with a coordinator item, but only within a single region. Cosmos DB wraps partition-scoped operations inside a stored procedure using a JavaScript continuation model — cross-partition writes get no atomic guarantee. Google Spanner is the only cloud database that delivers true global ACID with external consistency, using TrueTime (GPS + atomic clocks) to assign globally ordered timestamps and a commit-wait delay to guarantee causality across datacenters. MongoDB supports multi-document transactions on replica sets but carries measurable performance overhead and does not prevent write skew under snapshot isolation. The right choice depends on atomicity scope, latency tolerance, and operational cost — not on which database claims to be "ACID-compliant."

posts.title: Compare-and-Swap and Optimistic Locking: How Every Database Implements It
posts.subtitle: From the CMPXCHG CPU instruction to DynamoDB ConditionExpressions and Cassandra LWT — how CAS and optimistic locking work across every major database.
posts.brief: Compare-and-Swap (CAS) is the CPU-level atomic instruction that makes lock-free concurrency possible. Optimistic locking builds on it at the database layer: read freely, compute locally, write only if the record has not changed. Every major database — PostgreSQL, MySQL, DynamoDB, Redis, MongoDB, CockroachDB, and Cassandra — implements CAS semantics differently. Choosing the wrong implementation, or retrying naïvely, turns a 10ms write into a retry storm. This post explains the full stack from `CMPXCHG` to `ConditionExpression`.

posts.title: The Consistency Continuum: From Read-Your-Own-Writes to Leaderless Replication
posts.subtitle: Beyond 'Strong vs Eventual': Navigating the subtle trade-offs of distributed agreement.
posts.brief: In distributed systems, consistency is a spectrum of trade-offs between latency, availability, and correctness. By leveraging session-based patterns like Read-Your-Own-Writes and formal Quorum logic ($W+R > N$), architects can provide the illusion of strong consistency while maintaining the horizontal scale of eventual consistency.

posts.title: Consistent Hashing: Scaling Without Chaos
posts.subtitle: How do you distribute data across 100 servers so that adding a new server doesn't require moving...
posts.brief: Standard hashing (`key % N`) breaks when $N$ changes — adding or removing a server reshuffles almost all keys. Consistent Hashing maps both servers and keys onto a **ring** (0–360°). When a server is added, only its immediate neighbors' keys move, minimizing data migration.

posts.title: Azure Cosmos DB API Modes Explained: NoSQL, MongoDB, Cassandra, PostgreSQL, Gremlin, and Table
posts.subtitle: What each API can and cannot do — and the compatibility gaps that break production migrations
posts.brief: Cosmos DB's six API modes are wire-protocol compatibility layers over one shared ARS storage engine — except PostgreSQL (Citus), which is genuinely different. Every API emulates its native database incompletely, and those gaps are structural, not bugs. API mode is permanent and cannot be changed after account creation. NoSQL API is the only one with full Cosmos DB feature access. MongoDB API fails silently on complex aggregation pipelines. Cassandra API lacks materialized views and cross-partition transactions. PostgreSQL API is a managed Citus cluster — a different product entirely. Choose the right API before writing the first byte.

posts.title: Azure Cosmos DB Consistency Levels Explained: Strong, Bounded Staleness, Session, Consistent Prefix, and Eventual
posts.subtitle: What each consistency level actually guarantees — and the production pitfalls that happen when you get it wrong
posts.brief: Cosmos DB offers five consistency levels — Strong, Bounded Staleness, Session, Consistent Prefix, Eventual — each with precise, non-obvious internal mechanics. Session does not mean HTTP session; it means a client-side token that tracks what you have seen. Strong is unavailable with multi-region writes. Eventual allows genuinely out-of-order reads. Picking the wrong level costs you either correctness or throughput — and the bugs are silent.

posts.title: Dot Product in Machine Learning: The Engine Behind Similarity, Attention, and Neural Networks
posts.subtitle: From cosine similarity to scaled dot-product attention — how one operation powers modern AI
posts.brief: The dot product multiplies corresponding elements of two vectors and sums the results. In machine learning it does three critical jobs: it scores semantic similarity between embeddings, computes every activation in a fully connected layer, and generates the Q·Kᵀ score matrix that transformer attention uses to decide what to focus on. Normalising by vector magnitude turns it into cosine similarity; dividing by √d_k in attention prevents softmax saturation. Master this one operation and the internals of neural networks, transformers, and vector search all click into place.

posts.title: What are Hash Tables? Basics Explained
posts.subtitle: Hash Tables are the magic behind O(1) lookups. We explain Hash Functions, Collisions, and why the...
posts.brief: A hash table gives you near-O(1) lookups, inserts, and deletes by using a **hash function** to map keys to array indices. The tradeoff: collisions (when two keys hash to the same slot) must be handled, and a full hash table must be resized.

posts.title: How AI Coding Agents Work: Models, Context, Sessions, and Memory
posts.subtitle: Inside the architecture of Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, and Cursor: how agents use LLMs, manage context windows, handle sessions, and tier memory.
posts.brief: An AI coding agent is an LLM stapled to a tool registry, wrapped in an orchestration loop that painstakingly rebuilds state on every single API call — because the model itself is completely stateless. Understanding the context window, the ReAct loop, and the four-tier memory stack explains every hallucination, forgotten variable, and mid-refactor context dropout you've ever blamed on "the AI."

posts.title: How It Works: Thread Safety Internals of Java's ConcurrentHashMap
posts.subtitle: Explore volatile reads, Compare-And-Swap (CAS) loops, bucket-head locking, and parallel resizing in Java's map.
posts.brief: Java's `ConcurrentHashMap` achieves high read throughput and thread-safe writes by avoiding table-level locks. It utilizes lock-free `volatile` node reads and isolates write locking to individual bucket heads, allowing separate threads to write to different slots concurrently.

posts.title: How It Works: The Internals of Database B+ Tree Indexes
posts.subtitle: Understand how B+ Trees minimize disk I/O, manage page splits, and accelerate database queries.
posts.brief: Database indexes utilize B+ Trees to minimize slow disk I/O operations. By organizing data into balanced, wide node pages and linking leaf nodes sequentially, databases resolve queries in logarithmic time and support fast range scans.

posts.title: How GPT (LLM) Works: The Next Word Predictor
posts.subtitle: ChatGPT isn't magic; it's math. We explain the core mechanism of Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPT) and how they predict the next word.
posts.brief: At its core, GPT asks one question, repeated: *"Given everything so far, what is the most likely next token?"* Tokens are not words — they're subword units. The Transformer architecture uses **self-attention** to weigh how much each token should influence the prediction. Sampling strategies (temperature, top-p) control how creative or deterministic the output is.

posts.title: How Fluentd Works: The Unified Logging Layer
posts.subtitle: Logs are messy. Fluentd cleans them up. Learn how this open-source data collector unifies logging from multiple sources.
posts.brief: Fluentd is an open-source data collector that decouples log sources from destinations. It ingests logs from 100+ sources (Nginx, Docker, syslog), normalizes them to JSON, applies filters and transformations, and routes them to 100+ outputs (Elasticsearch, S3, Kafka). Tag-based routing is the core concept.

posts.title: How JVM Garbage Collection Works: Types, Memory Impact, and Tuning
posts.subtitle: From Minor GC to ZGC: how each Java garbage collector manages heap memory and what it means for your application's latency and throughput.
posts.brief: JVM garbage collection automatically reclaims unused heap memory, but every algorithm makes a different trade-off between throughput, latency, and memory footprint. The default G1GC targets 200ms pause goals and works well for most services. For sub-millisecond pauses on large heaps, use ZGC (Java 15+). For pure batch throughput, Parallel GC wins. Understanding heap regions — Eden, Survivor, Old Gen, Metaspace — tells you why `OutOfMemoryError` happens, what triggers a full GC, and which JVM flags to tune first.

posts.title: How Kafka Works: The Log That Never Forgets
posts.subtitle: Kafka is not just a message queue; it's a distributed streaming platform. We explain Topics, Partitions, and Offsets.
posts.brief: Kafka is a distributed event store. Unlike a traditional queue (RabbitMQ) where messages disappear after reading, Kafka stores them in a persistent **Log**. This allows multiple consumers to read the same data at their own pace, replay history, and handle massive scale via **Partitions**.

posts.title: How Kubernetes Works: The Container Orchestrator
posts.subtitle: Docker runs containers. Kubernetes manages them. We explain Pods, Nodes, Deployments, and Services to demystify the world's most popular orchestrator.

TLDR: Kubernetes (K8s) is an operating system for the cloud. It manages clusters of computers (Nodes) and schedules applications (Pods) onto them via a continuous declarative control loop — you

posts.title: How Apache Lucene Works: The Engine Behind Elasticsearch
posts.subtitle: Elasticsearch and Solr are built on Lucene. We explain the Inverted Index, Segments, and TF-IDF scoring.
posts.brief: Lucene is a search library. Its core innovation is the **inverted index** — a reverse map from words to documents, like the index at the back of a textbook. Documents are stored in immutable **segments** that Lucene merges in the background to keep queries fast. Elasticsearch is Lucene distributed across a cluster.

posts.title: How OAuth 2.0 Works: The Valet Key Pattern
posts.subtitle: Stop sharing your password. OAuth 2.0 lets you grant limited access to your data (like 'Read Contacts') without sharing your credentials.
posts.brief: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization protocol. It lets a third-party app (like Spotify) access your resources (like Facebook Friends) **without you giving it your Facebook password**. It uses short-lived **Access Tokens** as scoped, revocable keys.

posts.title: How It Works: Under the Hood of the Redis Single-Threaded Engine
posts.subtitle: Understand epoll multiplexing, memory layouts, ziplists, and eviction policies inside the Redis engine.
posts.brief: Redis achieves sub-millisecond latencies and millions of operations per second by executing all commands inside a single thread. This avoids thread context switching and lock contention, relying on non-blocking I/O multiplexing (`epoll`) to handle thousands of concurrent client sockets.

posts.title: How SSL/TLS Works: The Handshake Explained
posts.subtitle: When you see the green lock icon, your data is safe. But how? We break down the SSL Handshake, Public/Private Keys, and Certificates.
posts.brief: SSL (now TLS) secures data between your browser and a server. It uses **Asymmetric Encryption** (Public/Private keys) once — to safely exchange a fast **Symmetric Session Key**. Everything after the handshake is encrypted with the session key.

posts.title: How Transformer Architecture Works: A Deep Dive
posts.subtitle: The Transformer is the engine behind ChatGPT, BERT, and Claude. We break down Self-Attention, Mul...
posts.brief: The Transformer is the architecture behind every major LLM (GPT, BERT, Claude, Gemini). Its core innovation is **Self-Attention** — a mechanism that lets the model weigh relationships between all tokens in a sequence simultaneously, regardless of distance. This enables parallelism that RNNs could not achieve.

posts.title: X.509 Certificates: A Deep Dive into How They Work
posts.subtitle: Your browser trusts Google because of a file called a Certificate. We explain the Chain of Trust, Public Keys, and Revocation.
posts.brief: An X.509 Certificate is a digital document that binds a **Public Key** to an **Identity** (e.g., `google.com`). It is digitally signed by a trusted **Certificate Authority (CA)**. It prevents attackers from impersonating websites via man-in-the-middle attacks.

posts.title: Understanding Inverted Index and Its Benefits in Software Development
posts.subtitle: Why is Google so fast? It doesn't scan every webpage. It uses an Inverted Index. We explain how t...
posts.brief:
TLDR

TLDR: An Inverted Index maps every word to the list of documents containing it — the same structure as the back-of-the-book index. It is the core data structure behind every full-text search eng

posts.title: Java Memory Model Demystified: Stack vs. Heap
posts.subtitle: Where do your variables live? We explain the Stack, the Heap, and the Garbage Collector in simple terms.
posts.brief: Java memory is split into two main areas: the **Stack** for method execution frames and primitives, and the **Heap** for all objects. Understanding their differences is essential for avoiding stack overflow errors, memory leaks, and garbage collection pauses.

posts.title: Probabilistic Data Structures: A Practical Guide to Bloom Filters, HyperLogLog, and Count-Min Sketch
posts.subtitle: Trade exact answers for fixed memory and O(1) operations: a comparative guide to Bloom Filters, HyperLogLog, and Count-Min Sketch.
posts.brief: Probabilistic data structures trade a small, bounded probability of being wrong for orders-of-magnitude better memory efficiency and O(1) speed. Bloom Filters answer "definitely not in this set" in constant time with zero false negatives. HyperLogLog counts billions of unique elements in 12 KB with ±0.81% error. Count-Min Sketch estimates how often any element appeared in a stream using a fixed counter matrix. Each structure solves a different question — membership, cardinality, or frequency — at scales where exact answers are unaffordable.

posts.title: Python Data Structures: Lists, Dicts, Sets, and Tuples
posts.subtitle: Python's built-in collections aren't just syntax — their internals determine whether your code runs in O(1) or O(n)
posts.brief: Python's four built-in collections are not interchangeable — their internals are fundamentally different. `list` is a dynamic array: fast at the end, slow for membership. `dict` is a hash table: O(1) key lookup, insertion-order-preserving since Python 3.7. `set` is a hash set: O(1) membership, no duplicates, unordered. `tuple` is immutable and hashable: safe as a dict key, cheaper to create than a list. Pick the right one and a 30-minute batch job stays 30 minutes instead of turning into a 14-hour overnight disaster.

posts.title: Redis Sorted Sets Explained: Skip Lists, Scores, and Real-World Use Cases
posts.subtitle: Skip lists, dual indexing, and the five production patterns every backend engineer reaches for.
posts.brief: Redis Sorted Sets (ZSETs) store unique members each paired with a floating-point score, kept in sorted order at all times. Internally they use a **skip list** for O(log N) range queries and a **hash table** for O(1) score lookup — giving you the best of both. The five patterns you'll reach for most: leaderboards, social feed caches, sliding-window rate limiters, priority job queues, and expiring session stores.

posts.title: Spark Architecture: Driver, Executors, DAG Scheduler, and Task Scheduler Explained
posts.subtitle: Why your Spark job fails with OOM at the same stage every time — and how understanding the driver, DAG scheduler, and executors fixes it
posts.brief: Spark's architecture is a precise chain of responsibility. The Driver converts user code into a DAG, the DAGScheduler breaks it into stages at shuffle boundaries, the TaskScheduler dispatches tasks to Executors respecting data locality, and the Cluster Manager handles raw resource allocation. Understanding what each component does — and what kills it — is the difference between tuning Spark intentionally and tuning it by luck.

posts.title: Sparse Mixture of Experts: How MoE LLMs Do More With Less Compute
posts.subtitle: How MoE replaces the dense FFN with N expert layers and a learned router — GPT-4-scale capacity at a fraction of inference cost
posts.brief: Mixture of Experts (MoE) replaces the single dense Feed-Forward Network (FFN) layer in each Transformer block with **N independent expert FFNs** plus a **learned router**. Only the top-K experts activate per token — so total parameters far exceed active parameters. Mixtral 8×7B carries 47B total parameters but computes like a ~12.9B model per forward pass. GPT-4 is widely believed to use a similar architecture at much larger scale. The payoff: near-GPT-4-quality output at GPT-3.5-level inference cost.

posts.title: Types of Locks Explained: Optimistic vs. Pessimistic Locking
posts.subtitle: How do you prevent two users from editing the same record at the same time? We compare Optimistic Locking (Versioning) and Pessimistic Locking (Databa
posts.brief: Pessimistic locking locks the record *before* editing — safe but slower under low contention. Optimistic locking checks for changes *before saving* using a version number — fast but can fail and require retry under high contention. Choosing correctly depends on your write-conflict probability.

posts.title: Webhooks Explained: Don't Call Us, We'll Call You
posts.subtitle: Polling is slow and wasteful. Webhooks are event-driven callbacks that deliver data the moment something happens.
posts.brief: Webhooks let one system push event data to another the moment something happens. Instead of polling ("anything new?"), you expose an endpoint and the provider POSTs signed event payloads to you in near real-time. The key production requirements: signature verification, idempotency, async processing.

posts.title: Adapting to Virtual Threads for Spring Developers
posts.subtitle: Migrate your Spring Boot services from thread-pool exhaustion to JDK 21 virtual threads — the practical Spring developer guide
posts.brief: Platform threads (one OS thread per request) max out at a few hundred concurrent I/O-bound requests. Virtual threads (JDK 21+) allow millions — with zero I/O-blocking cost. Spring Boot 3.2 enables them with a single property. Avoid `synchronized` blocks wrapping I/O (they pin virtual threads to OS threads) and CPU-bound work inside virtual threads. For I/O-heavy Spring services, virtual threads are the most impactful JVM upgrade since Java 8 lambdas.

posts.title: Advanced AI: Agents, RAG, and the Future of Intelligence
posts.subtitle: Is an LLM a brain in a jar? To make it truly useful, we need to give it access to the world. This guide explains RAG and Agents.
posts.brief: Large Language Models are brilliant "brains in a jar." Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) hands them a constantly refreshed memory, while AI Agents give them tools to act in the world. Combined, they turn static knowledge into dynamic, goal-directed intelligence — the next frontier of practical AI.

posts.title: Advanced Graph Algorithms: Dijkstra, Topological Sort, and Disjoint Set Union (DSU)
posts.subtitle: Master shortest paths, dependency resolution, and cycle detection with robust Java solutions.
posts.brief: Graph algorithms are the backbone of networking, scheduling, and connection analysis. This guide explores Dijkstra's pathfinding, Topological Sorting for dependency resolution, and Disjoint Set Union (DSU) for cycle detection, complete with runnable Java code.

posts.title: AI Agents Explained: When LLMs Start Using Tools
posts.subtitle: An LLM can talk, but an AI Agent can *act*. We explain how Agents use the ReAct framework to brow...
posts.brief: A standard LLM is a brain in a jar — it can reason but cannot act. An **AI Agent** connects that brain to tools (web search, code execution, APIs). Instead of just answering a question, an agent executes a loop of Thought → Action → Observation until the goal is reached.

posts.title: AI Architecture Patterns: Routers, Planner-Worker Loops, Memory Layers, and Evaluation Guardrails
posts.subtitle: Production AI needs explicit routing, memory, execution, and evaluation layers rather than one loop.
posts.brief: A single agent loop is enough for a demo, but production AI systems need explicit layers for routing, execution, memory, and evaluation. Those layers determine safety, latency, cost, and traceability far more than model choice alone.

posts.title: ANN Index Types Explained: When to Choose Flat, HNSW, IVF, or IVF-PQ
posts.subtitle: A production-first guide to picking the right vector index for recall, latency, memory, and update patterns.
posts.brief: If your dataset is small and correctness is critical, use Flat. If you need high recall with low latency and enough RAM, use HNSW. If your corpus is huge and memory is your bottleneck, use IVF-PQ. Start with HNSW for most RAG systems, then move to IVF or IVF-PQ when scale and cost force compression.

articles.brief: An AI coding agent is an LLM stapled to a tool registry, wrapped in an orchestration loop that painstakingly rebuilds state on every single API call — because the model itself is completely stateless. Understanding the context window, the ReAct loop, and the four-tier memory stack explains every hallucination, forgotten variable, and mid-refactor context dropout you've ever blamed on "the AI."

articles.title: How Bloom Filters Work: The Probabilistic Set
articles.brief:
TLDR

TLDR: A Bloom Filter is a bit array + multiple hash functions that answers "Is X in the set?" in \(O(1)\) constant space. It can return false positives (say "yes" when the answer is "no") but ne

articles.title: How CDC Works Across Databases: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, and Beyond
articles.brief: A data engineering team at a fintech company built what they believed was a robust Change Data Capture pipeline: three source databases (PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Cassandra), Debezium connectors wired

articles.title: How GPT (LLM) Works: The Next Word Predictor
articles.brief: At its core, GPT asks one question, repeated: *"Given everything so far, what is the most likely next token?"* Tokens are not words — they're subword units. The Transformer architecture uses **self-attention** to weigh how much each token should influence the prediction. Sampling strategies (temperature, top-p) control how creative or deterministic the output is.

articles.title: How Fluentd Works: The Unified Logging Layer
articles.brief: Fluentd is an open-source data collector that decouples log sources from destinations. It ingests logs from 100+ sources (Nginx, Docker, syslog), normalizes them to JSON, applies filters and transformations, and routes them to 100+ outputs (Elasticsearch, S3, Kafka). Tag-based routing is the core concept.

articles.title: How JVM Garbage Collection Works: Types, Memory Impact, and Tuning
articles.brief: JVM garbage collection automatically reclaims unused heap memory, but every algorithm makes a different trade-off between throughput, latency, and memory footprint. The default G1GC targets 200ms pause goals and works well for most services. For sub-millisecond pauses on large heaps, use ZGC (Java 15+). For pure batch throughput, Parallel GC wins. Understanding heap regions — Eden, Survivor, Old Gen, Metaspace — tells you why `OutOfMemoryError` happens, what triggers a full GC, and which JVM flags to tune first.

articles.title: How Kafka Works: The Log That Never Forgets
articles.brief: Kafka is a distributed event store. Unlike a traditional queue (RabbitMQ) where messages disappear after reading, Kafka stores them in a persistent **Log**. This allows multiple consumers to read the same data at their own pace, replay history, and handle massive scale via **Partitions**.

articles.title: How Kubernetes Works: The Container Orchestrator
articles.brief:
TLDR

TLDR: Kubernetes (K8s) is an operating system for the cloud. It manages clusters of computers (Nodes) and schedules applications (Pods) onto them via a continuous declarative control loop — you

articles.title: How Apache Lucene Works: The Engine Behind Elasticsearch
articles.brief: Lucene is a search library. Its core innovation is the **inverted index** — a reverse map from words to documents, like the index at the back of a textbook. Documents are stored in immutable **segments** that Lucene merges in the background to keep queries fast. Elasticsearch is Lucene distributed across a cluster.

articles.title: How OAuth 2.0 Works: The Valet Key Pattern
articles.brief: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization protocol. It lets a third-party app (like Spotify) access your resources (like Facebook Friends) **without you giving it your Facebook password**. It uses short-lived **Access Tokens** as scoped, revocable keys.

articles.title: How SSL/TLS Works: The Handshake Explained
articles.brief: SSL (now TLS) secures data between your browser and a server. It uses **Asymmetric Encryption** (Public/Private keys) once — to safely exchange a fast **Symmetric Session Key**. Everything after the handshake is encrypted with the session key.

articles.title: How Transformer Architecture Works: A Deep Dive
articles.brief: The Transformer is the architecture behind every major LLM (GPT, BERT, Claude, Gemini). Its core innovation is **Self-Attention** — a mechanism that lets the model weigh relationships between all tokens in a sequence simultaneously, regardless of distance. This enables parallelism that RNNs could not achieve.

articles.title: X.509 Certificates: A Deep Dive into How They Work
articles.brief: An X.509 Certificate is a digital document that binds a **Public Key** to an **Identity** (e.g., `google.com`). It is digitally signed by a trusted **Certificate Authority (CA)**. It prevents attackers from impersonating websites via man-in-the-middle attacks.

articles.title: Understanding Inverted Index and Its Benefits in Software Development
articles.brief:
TLDR

TLDR: An Inverted Index maps every word to the list of documents containing it — the same structure as the back-of-the-book index. It is the core data structure behind every full-text search eng

articles.title: Java Memory Model Demystified: Stack vs. Heap
articles.brief: Java memory is split into two main areas: the **Stack** for method execution frames and primitives, and the **Heap** for all objects. Understanding their differences is essential for avoiding stack overflow errors, memory leaks, and garbage collection pauses.

articles.title: Probabilistic Data Structures: A Practical Guide to Bloom Filters, HyperLogLog, and Count-Min Sketch
articles.brief: Probabilistic data structures trade a small, bounded probability of being wrong for orders-of-magnitude better memory efficiency and O(1) speed. Bloom Filters answer "definitely not in this set" in constant time with zero false negatives. HyperLogLog counts billions of unique elements in 12 KB with ±0.81% error. Count-Min Sketch estimates how often any element appeared in a stream using a fixed counter matrix. Each structure solves a different question — membership, cardinality, or frequency — at scales where exact answers are unaffordable.

articles.title: Python Data Structures: Lists, Dicts, Sets, and Tuples
articles.brief: Python's four built-in collections are not interchangeable — their internals are fundamentally different. `list` is a dynamic array: fast at the end, slow for membership. `dict` is a hash table: O(1) key lookup, insertion-order-preserving since Python 3.7. `set` is a hash set: O(1) membership, no duplicates, unordered. `tuple` is immutable and hashable: safe as a dict key, cheaper to create than a list. Pick the right one and a 30-minute batch job stays 30 minutes instead of turning into a 14-hour overnight disaster.

articles.title: Redis Sorted Sets Explained: Skip Lists, Scores, and Real-World Use Cases
articles.brief: Redis Sorted Sets (ZSETs) store unique members each paired with a floating-point score, kept in sorted order at all times. Internally they use a **skip list** for O(log N) range queries and a **hash table** for O(1) score lookup — giving you the best of both. The five patterns you'll reach for most: leaderboards, social feed caches, sliding-window rate limiters, priority job queues, and expiring session stores.

articles.title: Spark Architecture: Driver, Executors, DAG Scheduler, and Task Scheduler Explained
articles.brief: Spark's architecture is a precise chain of responsibility. The Driver converts user code into a DAG, the DAGScheduler breaks it into stages at shuffle boundaries, the TaskScheduler dispatches tasks to Executors respecting data locality, and the Cluster Manager handles raw resource allocation. Understanding what each component does — and what kills it — is the difference between tuning Spark intentionally and tuning it by luck.

articles.title: Sparse Mixture of Experts: How MoE LLMs Do More With Less Compute
articles.brief: Mixture of Experts (MoE) replaces the single dense Feed-Forward Network (FFN) layer in each Transformer block with **N independent expert FFNs** plus a **learned router**. Only the top-K experts activate per token — so total parameters far exceed active parameters. Mixtral 8×7B carries 47B total parameters but computes like a ~12.9B model per forward pass. GPT-4 is widely believed to use a similar architecture at much larger scale. The payoff: near-GPT-4-quality output at GPT-3.5-level inference cost.

articles.title: Types of Locks Explained: Optimistic vs. Pessimistic Locking
articles.brief: Pessimistic locking locks the record *before* editing — safe but slower under low contention. Optimistic locking checks for changes *before saving* using a version number — fast but can fail and require retry under high contention. Choosing correctly depends on your write-conflict probability.

articles.title: Webhooks Explained: Don't Call Us, We'll Call You
articles.brief: Webhooks let one system push event data to another the moment something happens. Instead of polling ("anything new?"), you expose an endpoint and the provider POSTs signed event payloads to you in near real-time. The key production requirements: signature verification, idempotency, async processing.
